blocks.en: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

blocks.translation: Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds; and blessings and peace be upon our master Muhammad, the seal of the prophets, and upon his pure family and all his companions.
The servant in need of his Self-Sufficient Master, Abu al-Ikhlas Hasan al-Wafa'i al-Shurunbulali al-Hanafi, says:

Some of my dear friends — may Allah treat us and them with His kindness — asked me to compose an introductory work on acts of worship that would bring within the beginner's reach the issues scattered throughout the lengthy works. So I sought Allah's help and answered him, seeking the reward, mentioning only what the people of preference (tarjih) have affirmed to be sound, without excessive elaboration.
And I named it:
"Nur al-Idah wa-Najat al-Arwah" (The Light of Clarification and the Salvation of the Souls).
I ask Allah to make it of benefit to His servants and to make its usefulness enduring.
The waters with which purification is valid are seven:
[1] Rainwater (water of the sky),
[2] sea water,
[3] river water,
[4] well water,
[5] snow water,
[6] hail water,
[7] and spring water.
These waters are then divided into five categories:
[1] Pure and purifying without dislike: this is absolute (unmixed) water;
[2] Pure and purifying but disliked: it is water from which a cat or the like has drunk, while it is little in quantity;
[3] Pure but not purifying: it is water that has been used to remove ritual impurity or for an act of devotion — such as performing wuḍūʾ upon wuḍūʾ with that intention;
The water becomes "used" by the mere fact of its separating from the body.

Wuḍūʾ is not valid with water of trees or fruit — even if it came out by itself without pressing, according to the more apparent view — nor with water whose natural quality has been changed by cooking or by the predominance of something else over it.
Predominance, in the case of mixing with solid substances, is by causing the water to lose its thinness and free-flowing nature; and it does not harm…
(That is) the change of all its qualities by a solid substance, such as saffron, fruit, or tree leaves.

Predominance in liquids is established by the appearance of one quality of a liquid that has only two qualities, like milk which has color and taste but no smell; or by the appearance of two qualities of a liquid having three qualities, like vinegar.
And predominance in a liquid that has no (distinctive) quality, such as used water and rose-water whose scent has dissipated, is determined by weight.
So if two ratls of used water are mixed with one ratl of unrestricted (pure) water, ablution with it is not permissible.
And in the opposite case, it is permitted.
The fourth is impure water, and it is that into which an impurity has fallen while being stagnant and small in quantity.
Small (water) is that which is less than ten by ten (cubits), so it becomes impure by it even if no trace of it appears in it; or (likewise) if it was flowing and its trace appeared in it.
And the trace is taste, color, or smell.
The fifth is water whose purifying property is doubtful, and it is that from which a donkey or a mule has drunk.
Small (i.e. little) water, when an animal has drunk from it, is of four categories, and it is called su'r (leftover).
The first is pure and purifying, not disliked, and it is that from which a human, a horse, or an animal whose flesh is eaten has drunk.
The second is impure, its use is not permitted, and it is that from which a dog, a pig, or any of the predatory beasts such as the leopard or the wolf has drunk.

The third is that whose use is disliked when something else is available, and it is the leftover (saʾr) of the cat, the free-roaming hen, birds of prey such as the falcon, the peregrine, and the kite, and house-dwellers like the mouse—but not the scorpion.
The fourth is that whose purifying nature is doubtful, namely the leftover of the mule and the donkey; if one finds nothing else, he performs ablution with it, then performs tayammum, and then prays.
If vessels become mixed and most of them are pure, he investigates (tahaarrii) for ablution and drinking; but if most of them are impure, he does not investigate except for drinking.
Regarding mixed garments, he investigates regardless of whether most of them are pure or impure.

The small well is drained by the falling into it of any impurity, even if little, other than animal droppings—like a drop of blood or wine; or by the falling in of a pig, even if it comes out alive without its mouth touching the water; or by the death of a dog, sheep, or human in it; or by the swelling of an animal in it, even a small one.
Two hundred buckets are drawn out if draining it completely is not possible.
If a hen, cat, or the like dies in it, it is obligatory to draw out forty buckets.
And if a mouse or the like dies in it, it is obligatory to draw out twenty buckets.
That serves as purification for the well, the bucket, the rope, and the hand of the one drawing the water.
The well does not become impure due to camel-dung, droppings, or cow-dung, unless the observer deems it a large amount, or no bucket is free of a dropping.

Water is not spoiled by the droppings of pigeons or sparrows, nor by the death in it of creatures which have no flowing blood, such as fish, frogs, water-creatures, mosquitoes, flies, hornets, and scorpions.
Nor by the falling in of a human being or of an animal whose flesh is eaten, when it emerges alive and there is no impurity upon its body.
Nor by the falling in of a mule, a donkey, or birds and wild beasts of prey, according to the sound view.
If the saliva of the fallen creature reaches the water, it takes on its ruling.
Finding a dead animal in the well renders it impure for a day and night [retroactively], and for three days and their nights if it is swollen, when the time of its falling in is not known.

blocks.en: Section on Istinjāʾ (cleansing after relieving oneself)

blocks.translation: It is incumbent upon a man to perform istibrāʾ until the trace of urine ceases and his heart is at ease, according to his habit — whether by walking, clearing the throat, lying down, or other means; and it is not permissible for him to commence ablution until he is reassured that the dripping of urine has stopped.

Istinjāʾ is a Sunnah from impurity issuing from the two passages so long as it does not exceed the point of exit; if it exceeds it and is of the amount of a dirham, removing it with water becomes obligatory; and if it exceeds a dirham, washing it becomes a fard.
Washing what is at the outlet is obligatory when performing ghusl from janābah, menstruation, and post-natal bleeding, even if what is at the outlet is little.
He cleans himself with a cleansing stone or the like; washing with water is preferable, and the best is to combine water and stone, so he wipes first then washes.
It is permitted to restrict oneself to water alone or to the stone alone, and the sunnah is cleansing the area.
The number in stones is recommended but not a sunnah, so he cleans himself with three stones as a recommendation if cleansing is achieved with fewer.

The manner of istinja is that he wipes with the first stone from the front to the back, with the second from the back to the front, and with the third from the front to the back, when the testicles are hanging.
If they are not hanging, he begins from the back to the front.
The woman begins from the front to the back, for fear of soiling her private part.
Then he washes his hands first with water, then rubs the area with water using the inside of one, two, or three fingers if needed.
The man raises his middle finger above the others at the beginning of istinja, then raises his ring finger, and does not restrict himself to a single finger.
The woman raises her ring finger and middle finger together at the start, for fear of experiencing pleasure.
The one performing istinja exaggerates in cleansing until he removes the foul smell, and in relaxing the buttocks if he is not fasting.
When he finishes, he washes his hands a second time, and dries his buttocks before standing if he is fasting.
It is not permitted to uncover the awrah for istinja.
When the impurity exceeds its point of exit and exceeds...

If the impurity exceeds the size of a dirham, the prayer is not valid with it when he can find something to remove it; and he should contrive to remove it without uncovering his nakedness before anyone who could see him.

It is disliked to perform istinjā' with a bone, with food (whether for humans or animals), with baked brick, pottery, charcoal, glass, gypsum, anything venerated such as a piece of silk brocade or cotton, and with the right hand—except for an excuse.
He enters the lavatory with his left foot, seeking refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed before entering, then sits leaning on his left side, and does not speak.
It is disliked to face the qiblah or turn one's back to it—even within buildings—and to face the disc of the sun, the moon, or the direction from which the wind blows.
It is disliked to urinate or defecate in water, in the shade, in a burrow, on a road, or under a fruit-bearing tree; and to urinate while standing—except for an excuse.
He exits the lavatory with his right foot, then says: "Praise be to Allah who has removed harm from me and given me well-being."
The pillars of wuḍū' are four, and they are its obligatory acts:
The first: washing the face, the limit of which in length is from the beginning of the surface of the forehead to the bottom of the chin, and in breadth what is between the two earlobes.
The second: washing his hands together with his two elbows.
The third is washing his two feet together with his two ankles.
The fourth is wiping a quarter of his head.
Its cause is the permitting of that which is not lawful except by it, and that is its worldly ruling; while its otherworldly ruling is the reward in the hereafter.
The conditions for its being obligatory are eight:
Sanity,
puberty,
Islam,
the ability to use sufficient water,
the occurrence of ritual impurity,
the absence of menstruation,
and postnatal bleeding,
and the narrowness of time.
The conditions for its validity are three:
covering all the skin with purifying water,
the cessation of whatever nullifies it from menstruation, postnatal bleeding, and ritual impurity,
and the removal of whatever prevents water from reaching the body — such as wax and grease.
Washing the outer surface of the thick beard is obligatory, according to the most correct opinion upon which fatwa is given.
And it is obligatory to make water reach the skin in the case of a thin beard.
It is not obligatory to make water reach the hair that hangs down beyond the circle of the face, nor what is hidden of the two lips when they are closed.

If the fingers are pressed together, or the nail grows long and covers the fingertip, or there is on it something that prevents water such as dough, then washing what is beneath it becomes obligatory.
Dirt, flea droppings, and the like do not prevent (the validity of the washing).
It is obligatory to move a tight ring.
If washing the cracks of his feet would harm him, it is permitted to pass water over the medicine he placed in them.
Washing or wiping is not repeated over the location of hair after it has been shaved, nor is washing repeated upon clipping one's nails or moustache.
Eighteen things are sunnah in wudu':
[1] Washing the hands up to the wrists.
[2] Mentioning Allah's name at the beginning.
[3] Using the siwak at its beginning — even with the finger if it is unavailable —
[4] Rinsing the mouth three times — even with a single handful —
[5] Sniffing water into the nose with three handfuls,
Exaggerating in rinsing the mouth and inhaling water (into the nose) for one who is not fasting.
Running water through a thick beard with a handful of water from beneath it, and combing through the fingers (and toes).
Washing (each part) three times.
Wiping the entire head once.
Wiping the two ears, even with the water (used) for the head.
Rubbing (the limbs).
Performing (the washings) in immediate succession.
The intention.
Observing the order as Allah the Exalted stipulated in His Book.
Beginning with the right-hand limbs.
And (beginning with) the tips of the fingers.
And (beginning with) the front of the head.
Wiping the (back of the) neck—not the throat.
It is said that the last four (of these) are (merely) recommended.
Among the etiquettes of ablution are fourteen things:
Sitting in an elevated place.
Facing the qiblah.
And not seeking the help of another (in performing wudu).
And not engaging in worldly conversation.
And combining the intention of the heart with the utterance of the tongue.
And making the transmitted supplications.
And saying the basmala at washing each limb.
And inserting his little finger into the openings of his ears.
And moving his loose-fitting ring.
And rinsing the mouth and sniffing water with the right hand.
And blowing the nose with the left hand.
And performing wudu before the entry of the prayer time, for one who is not excused.
And pronouncing the two testimonies of faith after it.
And that he drink from the leftover of the wudu water while standing, and that he say: "O Allah, make me among those who repent, and make me among those who purify themselves."
Six things are disliked for the one performing wudu:
Wasting water.
And being too sparing with it.
And striking the face with the water.
And speaking with the speech of people,
And seeking help from someone else without an excuse,
And repeating the wiping three times with fresh water.
Ablution is of three categories:

The first is obligatory upon one in minor ritual impurity: for prayer — even if it be supererogatory —, for the funeral prayer, for the prostration of recitation, and for touching the Qur'an — even a single verse.
The second is required (wajib): for circumambulating the Ka'bah.

The third is recommended (mandub): for sleeping in a state of purity, and when one awakens from sleep; for continuance upon purity; for performing ablution upon ablution; after backbiting, lying, tale-bearing, and after every sin; and for reciting poetry, loud laughter outside of prayer, washing the dead and carrying him; for the time of every prayer; before the major ablution of janabah; for the junub when eating, drinking, sleeping, or having intercourse; for anger, for the Qur'an, for hadith and its narration, for studying knowledge, for the adhan, the iqamah, and the sermon; for visiting the Prophet — may Allah bless him and grant him peace —, for standing at Arafah, for the sa'y between Safa and Marwah, for eating camel meat, and to escape the disagreement of the scholars — as when one touches a woman.
Twelve things invalidate wudu:
Whatever exits from the two passages — except wind from the front passage according to the most correct view.
Childbirth, even without the sight of blood, invalidates it.
A flowing impurity coming out from other than the two passages, such as blood and pus.

Vomiting of food, water, clotted blood, or bile when it fills the mouth — meaning that which the mouth cannot close over except with difficulty, according to the most correct view; and the scattered amounts of vomit are combined together if their cause is the same.
Blood which overpowers the saliva or is equal to it.
Sleep in which the buttocks are not firmly settled on the ground.
The lifting of a sleeper's buttocks before he awakens, even if he does not fall, according to the apparent view.
Fainting.
Insanity.
Intoxication.
The loud laughter of an awake adult within a prayer containing bowing and prostration, even if he intentionally exits the prayer by it.
Touching a private part with an erect penis without a barrier.
Ten things do not invalidate wudu:
The appearance of blood that does not flow from its place.
And the falling of flesh without the flowing of blood, like the Madani vein which is called (rishteh).
And the exit of a worm from a wound, ear, or nose.
And the touching of a penis.
And [touching] a woman.
And vomit that does not fill the mouth.
And vomiting of phlegm — even if it is much.
And the swaying of a sleeper such that the shifting of his backside is possible.
And the sleep of one settled, even if leaning upon something such that he would fall were it removed — according to the apparent view in both cases.
And the sleep of one praying — even if bowing or prostrating — in the manner of the Sunnah.
And Allah is the Granter of success.
Ghusl is obligated by one of seven things:
The exit of semen to the outside of the body when it separates from its place with desire — without intercourse.
And the disappearance of the glans — or its measure from one whose [glans] is cut — in one of the two orifices of a living human.
And the ejaculation of semen by intercourse with a dead [female] or with an animal.
And the finding of thin water after sleep, when his penis was not erect at the time of sleep.
And the finding of wetness which he supposes to be semen after his recovery from intoxication or unconsciousness.
And by menstruation.
And postnatal bleeding.
Even if the aforementioned things occurred before [embracing] Islam, according to the more correct view.
And washing the deceased is obligatory as a collective duty (fard kifayah).
There are ten things from which ghusl is not required:
Madhi (pre-seminal fluid).
And wadi (post-urinal fluid).
And a wet-dream without wetness — and the woman in this is like the man according to the apparent narration.
And childbirth without the sight of blood after it, according to the correct view.
And insertion [of the penis] with a cloth that prevents the experience of pleasure.
And an enema.
And inserting a finger or the like into one of the two passages.
And intercourse with an animal.
Or with a dead woman, without ejaculation.
And intercourse with a virgin whose virginity is not removed, without ejaculation.
Eleven things are obligatory in the ritual bath (ghusl):
Washing the mouth,
and the nose,
and the body once,
and inside the foreskin if there is no difficulty in retracting it,
and the navel,
and any piercing that is not closed up,
and the inside of braided hair of a man absolutely — but not the inside of the braided hair of a woman, provided the water reaches its roots —,
and the skin under the beard — even if it is thick —,
and the skin under the moustache,
and the eyebrow,
and the outer private part.
Twelve things are sunnah in the ritual bath (ghusl):
Beginning with the mention of Allah's name (basmala),
And the intention.
And washing the hands up to the wrists.
And washing any impurity if it was on his body, by itself.
And washing his private parts — even if there is no impurity on them.
Then he performs wudu like his wudu for prayer, washing each part three times.
And he wipes the head, but delays washing his feet if he is standing in a place where water collects.

Then he pours water over his body three times — and if he immerses himself in flowing water or in water having its ruling, and remains there the duration of a wudu and ghusl, he has fulfilled the sunnah.
And he begins by pouring water on his head.
Then after that he washes his right shoulder, then the left.
And he rubs his body.
And he performs the washing consecutively.
The etiquettes of ghusl are the same as the etiquettes of wudu, except that he does not face the qibla, because he is usually uncovering his private parts.
And what is disliked in wudu is also disliked in it (ghusl).
Ghusl is sunnah for four things:
[1] the Friday prayer,
[2] the prayer of the two Eids,
[3] for entering ihram,
[4] for the pilgrim at Arafah after the sun's zenith.
Ghusl is recommended (mandub) in sixteen things:
[1] for one who embraces Islam while in a state of purity,
[2] for one who reaches puberty by age,
[3] for one who recovers from insanity,
[4] upon performing cupping (hijamah),
[5] upon washing a deceased person,
[6] on the night of Bara'ah (mid-Sha'ban),
[7] on the Night of Qadr if he witnesses it,
[8] for entering Makkah,
[9] (for entering) the city of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace),
[10] for the standing at Muzdalifah on the morning of the Day of Sacrifice,
And at Mecca for the tawaf al-ziyarah,
And for the eclipse prayer,
And the prayer for rain,
And for fear/panic,
And darkness,
And a violent wind.
It is valid by eight conditions:
The first is the intention: its reality is the heart's resolve upon the act, and its time is when he strikes his hand upon that with which he performs tayammum.
The conditions for the validity of the intention are three:
Islam,
Discernment,
And knowledge of what he is intending.
And for the validity of the intention of tayammum for prayer by means of it, one of three things is required:
Either the intention of purification,
Or [the intention of] permitting the prayer,
Or the intention of a specifically intended act of worship that is not valid without purity;
So he may not pray with it if he intends merely the tayammum, or intends it for reciting the Qur'an while not being in a state of major ritual impurity.

The second is the excuse permitting tayammum: such as his being a mile away from water even if within the city, illness, and cold from which he fears perishing or sickness when outside the city, fear of an enemy, thirst, need [of water] for kneading—not for cooking broth—lacking a vessel, fear of missing the funeral or Eid prayer—even as a continuation [of the imam]; but fear of missing Jumu'ah or the prayer time is not among the excuses.
The third is that the tayammum be with something pure of the genus of the earth—such as dust, stone, and sand—not with wood, silver, or gold.
The fourth is the complete covering of the area with the wiping.

The fifth is that he wipe with the entire hand or the greater part of it: so that if he wiped with two fingers it is not valid, even if he repeated until he covered the whole area—contrary to the wiping of the head.

The sixth is that it be with two strikes with the inner sides of the two palms, even in one location; and in place of the two strikes, the dust's contact with his body suffices when he wipes it with the intention of tayammum.
The seventh is the cessation of whatever negates it, such as menstruation, postnatal bleeding, and ritual impurity.
The eighth is the removal of anything that prevents the wiping from reaching the skin, such as wax and grease.
Its cause and the conditions of its obligation are as mentioned regarding wudu.
And its two pillars are:
Wiping the two hands.
And the face.

blocks.en: The sunnahs of tayammum are seven:

blocks.translation: The basmala at its beginning,
And the proper sequence,
And continuity (without interruption),
Bringing the two hands forward after placing them in the dust,
And drawing them back,
And shaking them off,
And spreading the fingers apart.
It is recommended to delay the tayammum for one who hopes to obtain water before the time expires.
Delaying is obligatory upon the promise of water, even if he fears having to make up the prayer.
Delaying is also obligatory upon the promise of a garment or a water-skin, as long as he does not fear having to make up the prayer.
Seeking water is obligatory up to a distance of four hundred paces if he reasonably supposes it is nearby and is safe; otherwise, it is not.

He is obligated to ask for water from someone who has it with him, if he is in a place where people are not stingy with it; and if the person will only give it for its standard price, he must buy it provided he has surplus beyond his necessary expenses.
He may perform with a single tayammum whatever obligatory and supererogatory prayers he wishes.
It is valid to perform it before the prayer time has entered.
If most of the body or half of it is wounded, he performs tayammum; but if the greater part is sound...
He washes it, and wipes the wounded part.
He does not combine between washing and tayammum.
And what invalidates it is: anything that nullifies wudu, and the ability to use sufficient water.
One whose both hands and both feet are amputated, if there is a wound on his face, prays without purification and does not repeat the prayer.

blocks.en: Chapter on Wiping over the Leather Socks (Khuffs)

blocks.translation: Wiping over the khuffs is valid for men and women in minor ritual impurity, even if they are made of something thick other than leather, whether they have a leather sole or not.
Seven conditions are required for the permissibility of wiping over the khuffs:
The first: putting them on after washing both feet, even if before completing the wudu, provided he completes it before any nullifier of wudu occurs.
The second: that they cover both ankles.
The third: the possibility of continuous walking in them; so wiping is not permissible on a khuff made of glass, wood, or iron.
The fourth: that each of them is free from a tear the size of three of the smallest toes of the foot.
The fifth (condition) is that the two khuffs remain firm on the feet without being tied.
The sixth is that they prevent water from reaching the body (foot).

The seventh is that there remain of the front of the foot the measure of three fingers of the smallest fingers of the hand; so if he lacks the front part of his foot, he does not wipe over his khuff, even if the heel of the foot is present.

The resident wipes for a day and a night, and the traveler for three days with their nights; the beginning of the period is from the time of the ritual impurity (occurring) after putting on the two khuffs.
If a resident wipes then travels before the completion of his (resident's) period, he completes the period of the traveler.
If the traveler becomes a resident after he has wiped for a day and a night, he removes (the khuffs); otherwise, he completes a day and a night.
The obligatory portion of the wiping is the measure of three fingers of the smallest fingers of the hand, upon the upper surface of the front of each foot.
Its sunnah is to draw the fingers, spread apart, from the tips of the toes to the shin.
Four things invalidate the wiping over the khuff:
Anything that nullifies the wudu;
Removing a khuff, even by the greater part of the foot coming out into the shaft of the khuff;
Water reaching most of one of the two feet inside the khuff, according to the sound view;
The expiration of the period, if he does not fear the loss of his foot from the cold;
After the latter three (causes), only the washing of his two feet is required.
Wiping is not permitted over a turban, cap, face-veil, or gloves.

When someone is bled, wounded, or has a broken limb and binds it with a cloth or splint, and he is unable either to wash or to wipe the limb, then it is obligatory to wipe over most of what binds the limb; and it suffices to wipe over what is exposed of the body between the bandages of the one who has been bled.

Wiping over the splint is like washing: it is not restricted to a specific period, nor is it required that the splint be applied while in a state of purity. It is permissible to wipe over the splint on one foot while washing the other; the wiping is not invalidated if the splint falls off before healing; it is permissible to replace it with another, and repeating the wiping over the new one is not obligatory, though doing so is preferable.

If a person has sore eyes and is instructed not to wash his eye, or if his nail breaks and he places medicine, gum, or gallbladder-skin upon it whose removal would harm him, he is permitted to wipe over it; and if the wiping itself would harm him, he leaves it altogether.
Intention is not required for wiping over the leather socks, the splint, or the head.

blocks.en: Chapter on Menstruation and Postnatal Bleeding

blocks.translation: Three kinds of blood issue from the vulva:
[1] Menstrual blood,
[2] postpartum bleeding (nifās),
[3] and dysfunctional bleeding (istiḥāḍah).
Menstruation is blood expelled by the womb of a pubescent woman, without there being any illness in her, nor pregnancy, and who has not reached the age of menopause.
The minimum of menstruation is three days, its average is five, and its maximum is ten.
Postpartum bleeding (nifās) is the blood that comes out following childbirth.
Its maximum is forty days, and there is no limit set for its minimum.
Istiḥāḍah is blood that falls short of three days, or exceeds ten in menstruation, or exceeds forty in postpartum bleeding.
The minimum period of purity separating two menstruations is fifteen days; and there is no limit for its maximum, except in the case of one who has become a sufferer of istiḥāḍah.
Eight things are forbidden by reason of menstruation and postpartum bleeding:
[1] prayer,
[2] fasting,
[3] reciting a verse of the Qur’an,
[4] touching it (the Qur’an) except with a covering,
[5] entering a mosque,
[6] circumambulation (ṭawāf),
[7] sexual intercourse,
[8] And enjoyment of what is below the navel down to below the knee.
When the blood ceases at the maximum period of menses or lochia, intercourse becomes permissible without performing the ritual bath.

It is not permissible, however, if the blood ceased before that (the maximum) but before the completion of her customary habit, unless she performs ghusl, or makes tayammum and prays, or the prayer becomes an obligation owed upon her.

That is when, after the cessation, she finds within the time in which the blood ceased a span sufficient for the ghusl and the opening takbir or more, yet she neither bathes nor makes tayammum until the prayer time goes out.
The menstruating and the post-partum woman make up the fast but not the prayer.
Five things are forbidden because of major ritual impurity (janabah):
[1] Prayer,
[2] Reciting a verse from the Qur'an,
[3] Touching it (the Qur'an) except with a cover,
[4] Entering a mosque,
[5] And performing tawaf.
Three things are forbidden for the person in minor ritual impurity (hadath):
[1] Prayer,
[2] Tawaf,
[3] And touching the Qur'an except with a cover.
The blood of istihadah is like a continuous nosebleed: it does not prevent prayer, nor fasting, nor intercourse.
The woman with istihadah, and one who has an excuse such as urinary incontinence or chronic diarrhea, performs wudu for the time of...
Every obligatory prayer (requires a new ablution), and with it they may pray whatever they wish of obligatory and supererogatory prayers.
The ablution of the excused person is invalidated only by the exit of the prayer time.

One does not become a person of excuse until the excuse encompasses a complete prayer time in which there is no interruption sufficient for performing ablution and prayer; this is the condition for it being established.
The condition for its continuance is that it occurs in every time after that, even if only once.
The condition for its cessation is the elapsing of a complete prayer time free of it.

blocks.en: Chapter on Filth and Purification from It

blocks.translation: Filth is divided into two categories:
[1] Heavy (severe),
[2] and light.

The heavy (severe) filth is such as wine, flowing blood, the flesh and hide of carrion, the urine of what is not eaten, the dung of dogs, the excrement and saliva of beasts of prey, the droppings of chickens, ducks, and geese, and whatever invalidates ablution by its exit from a human's body.
As for the light filth, it is such as the urine of horses, the urine of animals whose flesh is eaten, and the droppings of birds whose flesh is not eaten.

An amount equal to a dirham is pardoned of the heavy filth, and less than a quarter of the garment or body is pardoned of the light filth; and splashes of urine like the heads of needles are pardoned.
If an impure bed or impure earth becomes moist from the sweat of a sleeper or the wetness of a foot, and the trace appears...
If [there is a trace of] impurity on the body or foot, they become impure; otherwise, not.
Just as a dry pure garment does not become impure when wrapped in a wet impure garment, provided that the wet one would not drip if wrung.

Nor does a wet garment become impure by being spread upon dry impure ground from which moisture transferred to it, nor by a wind that blew over impurity and then struck the garment, unless a trace of it appears on it.
That which has been defiled by a visible impurity becomes pure by the removal of its substance, even if [done] only once, according to the correct view.
It does not matter if a trace remains whose removal is difficult; and [an item defiled with] non-visible [impurity is purified] by washing it three times and wringing it each time.
That which cannot be wrung is purified by washing it until one is reasonably certain of its purity.
Impurity is removed from a garment or the body by water and by every cleansing liquid, such as vinegar and rose water.
The leather sock and similar items are purified by rubbing off an impurity that has substance, even if it is wet.
The sword and the like are purified by wiping.
When the trace of impurity is gone from the ground and it has dried, prayer upon it is permissible, though tayammum may not be performed from it.
Whatever is on it of standing trees and herbage is purified by its drying out.
An impurity whose substance has been transformed becomes pure, such as when it turns into salt or is consumed by fire.
Dry semen is purified by rubbing it off the garment and the body, while wet semen is purified by washing it.

The hide of carrion is purified by actual tanning, such as with qaraẓ leaves, or by figurative tanning, such as dusting it with earth or exposing it to the sun—except the hide of swine and of human beings.
Legally prescribed ritual slaughter purifies the hide of other than...
[The milk] of an edible animal, not its flesh, according to the most correct view on which fatwa is given.
Everything in which blood does not flow does not become impure by death—such as hair, shorn feathers, horn, hoof, and bone—provided there is no fat in it.
Sinew is impure according to the correct view. The musk pod is pure like musk itself, and eating it is lawful.
Civet is pure, and the prayer of one who has perfumed himself with it is valid.
